notes.meaning: Israel gathered together at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting, which was the sacred tent used for worshiping God. The main battles were now over, and moving the camp from Gilgal to Shiloh placed God's sanctuary right near the center of the land. Setting up the sanctuary first showed that honoring the Lord belonged at the very heart of their life as a nation.

Seven of the twelve tribes had not yet received their permanent homeland. Judah and the sons of Joseph had already been given their territory, but the dividing of the land had paused during the move to Shiloh. These remaining tribes were lingering without having places of their own.

Joshua challenged the people for being slow to move in and take the land God had promised them. They had become comfortable living off the spoils of war and did not want to face new hardships. God gives great gifts to his people, but they must still step out in faith to receive them.

Joshua told the seven tribes to select three men from each tribe, making twenty-one men in all. He planned to send them across the remaining country to survey the towns and fields and write down a clear report. Choosing trusted leaders from the tribes ensured that everyone would see the survey as fair and honest.

The surveyors were instructed to divide the rest of the land into seven balanced portions. Judah's borders in the south and the house of Joseph's lands in the north were to remain untouched. Setting up seven fair portions in advance prevented arguing over who received the best land.

Joshua told the men to bring their written survey to Shiloh so he could cast lots before the Lord. Casting lots was a sacred way of letting God decide the outcome rather than human choice. Doing this at the entrance of the tabernacle showed that each tribe's boundary was decided by God himself.

The tribe of Levi did not receive a tract of land because their special share was serving God as priests. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh had already received their land east of the Jordan River from Moses. This left exactly seven tribes that still needed a territory.

Joshua gave the chosen men their final marching orders as they set out. He commanded them to walk through the land, make an accurate written map, and return to him. Then Joshua would cast lots in the presence of the Lord at Shiloh to distribute the shares.

The twenty-one surveyors traveled through the land and carefully recorded its cities and regions into seven parts on a scroll. God protected them from hostile Canaanites so that they completed their mission in safety. They brought the written record back to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh.

Joshua cast lots for the seven tribes in the presence of the Lord outside the tabernacle at Shiloh. God directed the choice so that each tribe received the portion mapped out for it. This brought a peaceful and orderly finish to dividing the land among the people.

The first lot drawn came out for the clans of Benjamin. Their portion lay right between the powerful southern tribe of Judah and the tribes of Joseph to the north. God's providence placed Benjamin next to his brother Joseph while also joining him closely to Judah.

Benjamin's northern border started at the Jordan River near Jericho and climbed westward through the hills past Beth-aven. From there it ran along the southern ridge of Luz, which is Bethel, and went down to Lower Beth-horon. This line matched the southern edge of Ephraim, creating a clear border between the two brother tribes.

From the hill near Beth-horon, the western border turned southward and ended at Kiriath-baal, which is Kiriath-jearim, a city of Judah. The phrase translated as sea refers to the western direction toward the Mediterranean Sea. This marked the western limit of Benjamin's allotment.

Benjamin's southern boundary started at Kiriath-jearim and ran eastward past the spring at Nephtoah. It passed along the Valley of Hinnom, just south of the Jebusite hill of Jerusalem, and led down to En-rogel. This line followed the exact northern border of Judah, showing that the two tribes met right at Jerusalem.

From En-rogel, the border curved north toward En-shemesh and went on to Geliloth across from the pass of Adummim. It then led down to the Stone of Bohan, a landmark named after a man from the tribe of Reuben. These known landmarks kept the boundary clear along the rough hill trails.

The southern line continued down the slopes into the Jordan Valley and passed north of Beth-hoglah. It came to an end at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, where the Jordan River flows in. This spot marked the southeastern corner of Benjamin's tribal land.

The eastern border of Benjamin was the Jordan River itself. These surrounding boundaries clearly defined the entire territory given to the clans of Benjamin. Although their land was small, God marked out every side of their inheritance.

These verses name the first group of eastern towns belonging to Benjamin, including Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel. Although Jericho's walls had been torn down, its surrounding district was still inhabited. Bethel was an ancient site made famous by Jacob's vision generations earlier.

The list of eastern settlements continues with Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba, making twelve cities with their villages. Geba was a notable stronghold that later played a major role in the days of King Saul. These fortified towns guarded Benjamin's northern and eastern slopes.

The second group of cities lay in the western and central hills, including Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Mizpeh, Chephirah, and Mozah. Gibeon had previously made a peace covenant with Joshua. Ramah and Mizpeh later became famous centers where Israel's judges and prophets gathered the people.

The catalog finishes with Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zelah, Haeleph, Jebus (which is Jerusalem), Gibeah, and Kiriath, totaling fourteen cities and their villages. Jerusalem sat right on the border between Benjamin and Judah, though Canaanite Jebusites still held the fortress at this time. Even though Benjamin's land was small, it contained some of the most significant cities in Israel's history.
